claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, toughness retention is governed by the degree of principal-element nanosegregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes intergranular crack initiation.
Grain-boundary nanosegregation causes a loss of fracture toughness.
Post-annealing cooling rate controls grain-boundary nanocluster formation in CrMnFeCoNi.
The initial material is a single-phase, equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
The initial alloy has grain sizes of tens of micrometers.
The as-annealed CrMnFeCoNi alloy naturally exhibits some elemental segregation.
Slower cooling permits diffusion and potential coarsening of grain-boundary segregates.
Faster or uncontrolled cooling promotes rapid segregation of key elements to grain boundaries.
Cooling conditions that minimize or homogenize grain-boundary segregates preserve grain-boundary strength.
Reducing detrimental grain-boundary nanosegregation through modified cooling will increase fracture toughness relative to standard cooling.
Reducing grain-boundary nanosegregation will delay intergranular cracking.
The proposed behavior applies to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys such as CrMnFeCoNi.
The proposed toughness mechanism applies at ambient or moderate testing temperatures.
Deformation-induced twinning may also contribute to the toughness response.

contradictions.description: The cooling-rate direction is internally ambiguous: slower cooling is said both to allow diffusion and coarsening of segregates and to minimize rapid nanosegregation, while faster cooling is asserted to promote segregation. No consistent kinetic rationale identifies which cooling protocol should reduce the measured grain-boundary clusters.

The conditions specify tensile testing as the toughness measurement, whereas the predicted and falsification outcomes require fracture toughness/KIC. A conventional tensile test measures strength and ductility, not standardized KIC.
